The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', except two functional methods whose \KWD{self}
parameters stand at different positions, which only its code generator
refuses, as a malformed overload set (row~707 of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
====
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation.
Since the amendment of 14~October 2026 the interpreter checks the same at load,
at each object without static parameters, reading \KWD{comprises} clauses as its
check of the Meet Rule reads them: it accepts an object whose definitions at
narrower parameter types together cover an inherited abstract method, as before,
and refuses one whose definitions do not cover it, where it accepted any one
definition at narrower parameter types before.
It does not check objects with static parameters and object expressions in
generic functions (row~665 of the revival's gap ledger), and it
does not refuse an object where its search through the \KWD{comprises} clauses
does not settle: a cycle, its bound on steps or parts, or a type it cannot read;
it then loads an object that the compiled type checker refuses (row~708 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The compiled type checker does not split a tuple of parameter types through
\KWD{comprises} clauses: it refuses an object whose concrete methods cover an
inherited abstract method of two parameters only through combinations of the
types that a trait lists, which the interpreter accepts (row~709 of the
revival's gap ledger).

    msg: String := "no exception"
    try
        ignore(f())
    catch e
        UncheckedException => msg := e.asString
    end
    msg
  end

run(): () = do
    three = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#3}
    one = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 9}
    five = {[\ZZ32\] widen(5) |-> 5}
    all4 = {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(1) |-> 1, widen(2) |-> 2, widen(5) |-> 5}
    assert(three UPLUS five, all4, "a many-entry map UPLUS a one-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(five UPLUS three, all4, "a one-entry map UPLUS a many-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(overlap(fn () => one UPLUS three), "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 1 |-> 1 and |-> 9", "a one-entry map UPLUS a many-entry map holding its key throws KeyOverlap")
    assert(overlap(fn () => three UPLUS one), "no exception", "today's value: a many-entry map UPLUS a one-entry map holding its key throws nothing")
    assert(three UPLUS one, three, "today's value: a many-entry map UPLUS a one-entry map holding its key keeps the many-entry map's entries")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

content.content:
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
The object defines the method by a body at its parameter type, or by bodies at
narrower parameter types that together cover it, \KWD{comprises} clauses read
at the level of values (\secref{trait-decls}), as
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.
\end{Fortress}
For the latter, the programmer must provide a
definition for every type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of
\TYP{Molecule}, or definitions that together cover those types, or
it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here for a
definition for every immediate subtype of \TYP{Molecule}.
Where a trait with static parameters stands unlisted between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, the immediate subtypes and the
listed types differ; the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012) asks
for definitions for all the types comprised.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation of the revival.}

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.
Matching ignores case, backticks and double quotes, reads curly quotes as

## 5. Restatement

1. **Where.** A library extension goes into the one library: `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, the interpreter's. It never goes into a library tree of our own. It never goes into the compiler's prelude (the `Compiler*` files), which takes no new declaration and is deleted at the switch-over. *Rests on:* "need to go directly to the standard library" (09-19 18:31), and the one-library decision (09-20 14:39, 09-21 02:40).
2. **What qualifies.** A gap that the library's own text shows: it has an operation or a clause for one number type, rank or sibling trait, and lacks it for another. Write the missing one in the shape of the one it has, and cite that line. Study the library's existing parts first. On record: `02d09a39f` gave the integer scalar block to every number type and rank, gave `Array3` the ring exclusion that `Vector` and `Matrix` carry, and gave `AdditiveGroup` the marker that `AnyMultiplicativeRing` is; a `ReadableArray2` after `ReadableArray1` is approved for later (`POSITIONS.md:79`). *Rests on:* "study the existing parts of the fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns" (09-19 18:31); "As long as the extensions that we did have a precedent in the library itself, I, I'm fine with that. Like, if we are taking patterns from natural numbers or in, in integers and extending them to float, that's perfect." (09-20 07:20); "small defects in the library" (09-20 13:57); his "agreed" of 09-24 18:30.
3. **Why.** The model's need is the occasion, not the reason. A form that only the model uses, with no such precedent, stays in the model's own vocabulary, as the diagonal did. Moving one into the library is his decision, put to him with the library's own way first. *Rests on:* "I don't want that we extend the library f with some uh, forms that are specific to our use case in C4" and "It must be the other way around" (09-20 07:20); the diagonal kept in `FlatArrays` (09-24 18:30, `POSITIONS.md:79`).
4. **Who judges.** He does, one extension at a time, shown its precedent line. *Rests on:* "I want to specifically know what was moved to the standard library, and I want to be judge of whether it is like" (09-20 07:20); the blind review and his approvals change by change (09-21 02:26 and 17:08).
5. **What stays fixed.** The model's text is not changed to fit: its operators stay operators. The edit is made test first, like any edit of the original tree. *Rests on:* "That's not Fortress!" (09-19 18:13), and the test-first rule of 09-17 (`POSITIONS-history.md:25`).

A bullet for the skill at its next revision, in place of `library.md:30`:

> - Extend this library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`; not the `Compiler*` files) where it has an operation or a clause for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks it for another. Write the missing one in the shape of the one it has, and cite that line as its precedent: an integer form given to every number type, a rank-2 clause given to rank 3. A program's need, the model program's included, is the occasion for such a change, not its reason. Never put it into a library tree of our own. A form that only the model uses and that has no such precedent stays in the model's own components; if you think it belongs in the library, report it as a decision not taken. Name each extension and its precedent line in your report, for the curator to judge.

`library.md:31`, "Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it", then reads with "gap" in the sense of point 2.

59:## When to run a whole suite
60-
61-- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
62-- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
63-  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
64-  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
65-  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
66-- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
67-- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
68-- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
69-- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. the interpreter, and the compiled type checker when it checks \library, read
such a parameter as bounded by \TYP{Any}.
The type group's paper of 2019 gives the same default: ``By default, each type
parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom'' (Park, Hong, Steele
and Ryu, POPL 2019, Section~3.2).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any}, the restriction on a naked type parameter of
bound \TYP{Any} would forbid overloading every functional whose single
parameter's type is a type parameter declared without a bound, \library's
factory \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()} among them;
the compiled type checker applies the restriction only to a bound written
\TYP{Any}, and draws no such refusal on \library.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The type parameter of \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}} may be instantiated with
\TYP{(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z})} or \TYP{\mathbb{Z}}.  If this is the
case then the call \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}(3, 4)}, where 3 and 4 have type
\TYP{\mathbb{Z}}, is ambiguous.
A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, whose bound is
\TYP{Any} as well (\secref{type-param}), does not fall under this restriction:
\library\ declare the factory
\EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()}.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 stated this
restriction for a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} while a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause was bounded by \TYP{Object}
(\secref{type-param}).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any} it would forbid overloading every functional
whose single parameter's type is such a type parameter, the factory above among
them.

## 1. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`). At the **switch-over** the compiled path takes it over.
- **The distance** is the number of errors the checker reports on the one library. Each error has a **site** (a file and a line). This record counts sites by the ledger **row** that records their defect.
- **The count** is the older measure: the checker's errors on the one library until a component's first thrown error stops it. It is 1: `__bigOperator`'s local `body(i)`, whose parameter has no type.
- A **row** is an entry of the gap ledger, cited by number. An **item** is a numbered question in PLAN's list "Pavol's answers".
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a second worker, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs, merged and tested together by the **gate** and landed at once.
- **Test first.** Every fix starts with a test that shows the defect, seen failing before the edit and passing after. An **expected failure** is a test named `XXX...` that passes while the defect is there; when the fix lands it is **promoted** to a plain name.

## 5. How it is run

The batch runs on the workflow of batch 14: `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, its manual `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, and the practice they build, `coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`. content.content:
12:**`XXX` test**
44:- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.
70:## How `XXX` works
72:- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
73:- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
75:- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
76:- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
77:- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.
83:1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
84:2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
101:## Writing an `XXX` test
103:In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.
105:- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
106:- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
108:  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
109:  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
